title: Skill issue: stop deploying vision language models, use them with Skills — Merve Noyan, Hugging Face
talk_summary: Merve Noyan argues developers should stop using vision-language models directly for vision tasks and instead use them as tools (labeler + ensemble judges) inside a pipeline that trains small task-specific Apache-2.0 models like RFDTR. She shows a coding agent babysitting this long-horizon pipeline, with concrete findings on judge imbalance, prompt generation, and agent common-sense failures.

takeaways.technique: Ensemble small judges with minimum-agreement merge instead of single judge or consensus
takeaways.what_they_do: Two differently-sized VLM judges (Gemma ~8B, LFM ~2B) each accept/reject labeled examples; an example is kept if either judge approves (minimum agreement), because strict consensus discarded too much data and hurt generalization.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if one of them says yes, I'm going to take that example and nevertheless it worked well
takeaways.numbers: Consensus filtering left 'very very little number of examples' and poor generalization; minimum-agreement worked well

takeaways.technique: Don't trust scalar LLM judge scores across model sizes; use binary verdicts or IoU
takeaways.what_they_do: She found numeric scores from judges are unreliable, especially when judges differ in size, and instead uses accept/reject verdicts (and plans IoU between judge boxes and labels).
takeaways.evidence_quote: most of the people ask the VLM or LLM to assign some score to it but those scores absolutely absolutely don't work

takeaways.technique: Coding agent as pipeline babysitter for long-horizon jobs
takeaways.what_they_do: A coding agent (Opus then GLM 5.2) drives the whole label→judge→train pipeline end-to-end from a repo, handling infra calls; she notes GLM did well on long-horizon tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: ran the workflow with the G gl GLM 5.2 2 which is doing a good job on long horizon tasks

takeaways.technique: Package domain expertise as Skills/toolkits for coding agents
takeaways.what_they_do: She ships a 'web vision' toolkit of curated models-as-tools plus HF skills so a coding agent that is 'clueless' in the domain can still execute correctly; she distills her own model-selection criteria (license, benchmarks, vibes) into it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your coding agent is a bit of a clueless computer vision engineer basically

takeaways.technique: Human approval only at the one irreducible checkpoint
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent generates judge prompts and label descriptions automatically; the human only reviews/approves those generated prompts, which she identifies as the single unavoidable human step.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this is the only part where as a human you have to approve

takeaways.technique: Cheap serverless/batch for bulk steps, small models for training
takeaways.what_they_do: She routes labeling to cheap serverless (DeepInfra), judging to batch jobs, and training to a small L4 because the target model is tiny; total pipeline cost is a few dollars.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for the judging I used hugging face jobs which cost less
